issues.legal_issue: A challenge to a judicial assignment that was not pursued before the judge or chief justice does not, merely by being repeated in a special leave petition, disentitle the petitioner from pursuing that petition.
material_facts: A party made a representation to the chief justice seeking a different judge to hear the matter and sent a copy to the judge whose order was challenged.
The party did not pursue the representation before the judge or chief justice and did not raise the concern before the hearing concluded.
The party repeated the circumstances of the representation in the special leave petition.
The opposing party argued that the petition should not be entertained because of the party's conduct.
issues.conclusion: The preliminary objection was overruled; repeating the concern in the petition did not disentitle the party from filing it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held on these circumstances that a mere reiteration of an unpursued concern about the appropriateness of a judge hearing a matter does not bar a special leave petition.

predicates.special_leave_petition_challenges_court_: A party seeks special leave to challenge a court order.
predicates.judicial_assignment_concern_was_raised_i: A party made a representation raising concern about which judge would hear the matter.
predicates.concern_not_pursued_before_judge_or_chie: The party did not pursue the concern before the judge or the chief justice and did not raise it before the hearing concluded.
predicates.concern_repeated_in_petition: The party repeated the circumstances of the concern in the petition.
predicates.preliminary_objection_overruled: The objection that the petition should not be entertained is rejected.

issues.definition: When a special leave petition challenges a court order and repeats an assignment concern that was not pursued before the judge or chief justice, the objection to entertaining the petition is overruled.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court cannot use revisional jurisdiction to overturn an appellate court's refusal to admit additional evidence merely because better scientific examination is available, when the appellate court does not require that evidence to decide the appeal.
material_facts: In an appeal from a decree, the parties sought permission to have documents examined by a forensic laboratory with facilities for detecting erasures.
The requested laboratory facility was not available at the time of trial, and the trial court had not refused to admit evidence that ought to have been admitted.
The first appellate court refused the request to adduce additional evidence.
The High Court, in revision, reversed that refusal after considering the availability of the laboratory facility and whether its later availability was sufficient cause.
The whole appeal was not before the High Court in the revision proceeding.

The Supreme Court held that the first appellate court had not found the additional evidence necessary and that better scientific evidence could not justify an unending process of adducing further evidence at successive stages.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have interfered in revision. The Supreme Court set aside its order and restored the first appellate court's refusal, while leaving the parties free to challenge that refusal in the pending appeal if permitted by law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 107 CPC permits an appellate court to take additional evidence only subject to Order XLI, Rule 27 CPC. Under Rule 27, additional evidence may be admitted if the court below refused evidence that ought to have been admitted; if, despite due diligence, the evidence was unknown or could not have been produced when the decree was passed; or if the appellate court requires it to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause. Admission is not a party's right and is a discretion to be exercised judiciously and sparingly. The phrase 'for any other substantial cause' is limited by the requirement that the appellate court require the evidence. A lacuna or defect in the existing evidence that prevents a satisfactory judgment may justify admission, but mere difficulty in deciding or the availability of better scientific evidence does not. These principles are supported by Kesowji Issur v. G.I.P. Railway, AIR 1931 PC 143; Syed Abdul Khader v. Rami Reddy, AIR 1979 SC 553; The Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Lala Pancham, AIR 1965 SC 1008; and Gurdev Singh v. Mehnga Ram, (1997) 6 SCC 507. Where the first appellate court has refused additional evidence and does not require it to decide the appeal, the High Court should not reverse that decision in revision, particularly when the appeal itself is not before it.

rule.if: appeal_from_decree and additional_evidence_sought_on_appeal and first_appellate_court_refused_request and first_appellate_court_found_existing_record_sufficient and high_court_reversed_refusal_in_revision and entire_appeal_not_before_high_court

predicates.appeal_from_decree: The proceeding in which the request for further evidence is made is an appeal from a decree.
predicates.additional_evidence_sought_on_appeal: A party asks the appellate court to receive further evidence.
predicates.first_appellate_court_refused_request: The first appellate court rejects the party's request for further evidence.
predicates.first_appellate_court_found_existing_rec: The first appellate court considers the evidence already on the record sufficient to decide the matter.
predicates.high_court_reversed_refusal_in_revision: The High Court uses revision to reverse the first appellate court's refusal.
predicates.entire_appeal_not_before_high_court: The appeal itself is not before the High Court when it considers the request in revision.
predicates.revisional_interference_with_refusal_is_: The High Court's reversal of the refusal in revision is improper.

issues.definition: When, in an appeal from a decree, the first appellate court refuses further evidence because the existing record is sufficient, the High Court reverses that refusal in revision, and the appeal itself is not before the High Court, that revisional interference is improper.
